extracted.intended_audience: general educated readers and actuarial / life-insurance professionals
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on constructing, interpreting, and comparing mortality tables and life-insurance experience data, including data-quality requirements, selection effects, and the influence of epidemics and registration practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient sample size and observation period
rubrics_metrics.description: Large numbers must be observed for a long term of years, to have deaths occur for every single year of life, and in the proper proportion for each age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the Carlisle table example: with only 230 deaths per year small samples produce missing deaths at many ages and large random fluctuations; mathematicians must estimate probable percentages for each year of life when raw data are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graduation/adjusting to determine the law of mortality
rubrics_metrics.description: The process of removing unevennesses in the observed mortality curve (called graduating or adjusting) to determine the underlying law of mortality freed from accidental influences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The outline of the law is clear (high infant mortality, minimum near puberty, gradual rise, rapid increase in old age), but details are disturbed by accidental causes; graduation is a delicate and important problem to trace the true trend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representativeness of the underlying population
rubrics_metrics.description: Life tables derived from different populations (whole-population censuses vs. insured lives) reflect different social conditions and must be compared with care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: English Life Table No. 3 (population-based) vs Actuaries' Experience and American Experience Tables (insured classes) — differences arise because insurers select healthier, better-class individuals, so tables are context-dependent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of selection bias in insurance data
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection (medical examination and choosing healthier applicants) initially reduces observed mortality, but the effect nearly wears away in about five years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While diseased persons are excluded at entry, many selected sound lives will decline in health over years; reexamination after several years would show selection advantages largely disappeared.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misrepresentation and fraud among applicants
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempts by the public to foist impaired lives on insurers (misrepresentation) reduce the apparent standard of health in insurance data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No amount of care can detect all misrepresentation; this undetected fraud undoubtedly reduces the standard of absolute health in insurer experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact of lapses on experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy lapses (policies allowed to terminate) tend to remove many healthy lives and leave a disproportion of the sickly, degrading the average mortality experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Healthy policyholders often forfeit their insurance for slight reasons, whereas those who think their health impaired tend to retain policies; the remaining pool can thus show worse mortality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects of epidemics on average mortality
rubrics_metrics.description: Epidemics may raise mortality markedly in a given year but can be followed by lower-than-average mortality because many weak and sickly have been removed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: cholera 1849 raised deaths that year but five-year averages remained roughly unchanged; epidemics chiefly affect the poor and crowded quarters (who largely do not insure), so insurer experience may be less impacted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of frequent and comprehensive registration/census
rubrics_metrics.description: More frequent and complete registration (ideally annual census and vital registration) yields better data for computing life tables and reduces the need for mathematical speculation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decennial census (introduced 1801) and registration (from 1836) were important steps; an annual census is urged to allow closer and more frequent examination of facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small-sample fluctuations at extreme ages
rubrics_metrics.description: Very small numbers of insured at very young and very old ages produce large percentage fluctuations and sometimes zero deaths recorded at particular ages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ungraded Actuaries' Table No. 2 showed no deaths at ages 11, 16, and 94 out of 23,800 deaths — an artifact of insufficient numbers at those ages, causing apparent irregular spikes or falls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mortality differences by sex and age-pattern interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Tables should record and allow comparison of male and female mortality; notable patterns (e.g., females often having better survival except in certain age ranges) must be analyzed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: English Life Table No. 3 shows females have better chances of life except between 15 and 37 where physiological causes explain higher female mortality; birth and survival ratios vary by country and social conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tables are approximate and time-/condition-dependent
rubrics_metrics.description: Every graduated mortality table is only an approximate expression of the death-rate under the conditions and at the time of observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There may be a fundamental law of life but it is frequently traversed by artificial and accidental influences; life-tables must be interpreted as approximate and contingent on contemporaneous social conditions.
